title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching
abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid misalignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose conebeam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain selfsupervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

title: EgoExplorer: A Vision-Motion-Touch Observatory for Human Loco-Manipulation In Situ
abstract: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation from human demonstrations rests on observing how locomotion, posture, and object interaction evolve together as tasks unfold. Scaling collection across diverse environments, in turn, favors lightweight, portable capture systems. Yet, existing datasets provide only partial views of this coordination. Thus, we introduce EgoExplorer, a 100-hour vision-motion-touch observatory of human loco-manipulation built with a wearable system. With an emphasis on professional activities, its continuous recordings align egocentric video with reconstructed whole-body motion, fine-grained finger articulation, and tactile observations, accompanied by step-level descriptions. To achieve this coverage with sparse body sensing, we develop the Calibrate-Complete-Constrain pipeline. Concretely, reusable calibration fixes participant geometry and sensor attachments before motion inference to disentangle mounting offsets from articulation. A temporal prior then completes unobserved joint motion, while layered constraints promote measurement agreement, temporal continuity, and geometric consistency, properties that motion plausibility alone does not guarantee. Against tracker-fitted references, the method reduces body-point error by 71.9% relative to the strongest baseline; matched evaluations also show gains in hand stability and contact estimation. Preliminary studies explore multimodal generation and conditioning alongside humanoid retargeting with whole-body control in simulation.

title: Beyond ICD Codes: Semantic IDs for Generative Medical Coding
abstract: Generative approaches to automatic International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding use large language models (LLMs) to predict ICD codes from clinical documents. However, original ICD code strings are not ideal generation targets because the ICD hierarchy does not always reflect clinical relationships, and LLMs struggle to interpret and generate these codes. We introduce SemICD, a framework that trains LLMs to generate Semantic IDs (SIDs) instead. SemICD constructs SIDs by hierarchically clustering embeddings of textual code profiles, allowing semantically related codes to share prefixes while each complete SID uniquely identifies one ICD code. To align the SID tokens with clinical semantics, we employ two auxiliary tasks for bidirectional generation between textual code profiles and SIDs. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLMs show that SemICD outperforms direct code generation, improving Micro-F1 by 1.34-8.00 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/youwillbethebest/SemICD.

title: MIND: Instruction-Conditioned Incremental Grounding for Robots
abstract: Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target-room decisions without re-evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 evaluations against 15 to 18. Additional materials are available at https://mind-icra27.github.io/.

title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.

title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

title: Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion
abstract: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/

title: Mapping AI Adoption in Digital Marketing: A Bibliometric Analysis, Systematic Literature Review, and Future Research Agenda
abstract: This study aims to map the development of artificial intelligence adoption in digital marketing, identify dominant themes, examine methodological approaches, theoretical foundations, and empirical contexts, and formulate research gaps and a future research agenda. The study employs a combined design integrating bibliometric analysis and a systematic literature review. Data were obtained from 94 articles published during 2018–2026 and selected through the stages of identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. Bibliometric analysis was used to examine publication trends, journals, countries, citations, collaboration, and relationships among keywords, while VOSviewer was used to generate network visualization, density visualization, and overlay visualization. The results show that publications have grown rapidly, with a temporary peak in 2025. Dominant themes include artificial intelligence, digital marketing, machine learning, social media, generative AI, customer experience, trust, transparency, privacy, and personalization. Previous studies have been dominated by quantitative approaches, cross-sectional designs, and SEM analysis, with Signaling Theory being one of the most frequently used theoretical foundations. The main gaps include inconsistent definitions of AI adoption, limited longitudinal designs, weak integration of technical, organizational, and behavioral aspects, and limited attention to responsible AI and negative consequences. This study concludes that AI adoption in digital marketing should be understood as a gradual, multidimensional socio-technical process requiring the integration of technological capabilities, organizational readiness, consumer responses, and ethical governance.

title: Le Chapeau: An A/B Testing Platform for Socratic AI in Education
abstract: Le Chapeau is a turnkey experimental platform designed for educational and behavioral researchers to deploy controlled web chat applications comparing AI interaction paradigms (such as baseline control, direct instructional assistant, and Socratic questioning tutor) with real-time data persistence and salted deterministic anonymization.

title: raefalizadehnima-droid/Sustainable-Pathways-to-Trustworthy-AI-in-Pharmaceutical-Manufacturing: XAII
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is growing in pharmaceutical manufacturing, but regulatory assimilation has been slow due to difficulties in interpretability, uncertainty calibration and sustainability assessment. This work proposes a quantitative framework for assessing trustworthy AI through a multi-objective Composite Trust Index (CTI). The framework combines model predictive performance (R², RMSE), uncertainty measures (predictive variance and Expected Calibration Error), interpretability stability and sustainability metrics such as Process Mass Intensity (PMI), and is formulated for four AI paradigms: explainable AI (XAI), human-in-the-loop (HITL), hybrid physics-informed AI and uncertainty quantification (UQ).

title: 6G-HW10: 6G-Oriented Heterogeneous Waveform Dataset
abstract: 6G-HW10: 6G-Oriented Heterogeneous Waveform Dataset 6G-HW10 is a controlled synthetic dataset for heterogeneous waveform and modulation recognition from short complex-baseband observations. It combines traditional single-carrier modulation schemes, OFDM-based waveforms, OTFS-like and AFDM-like constructions, and a two-user downlink NOMA superposition under shared channel and RF-impairment parameter distributions. Key Features • Ten classes: BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK, QAM16, QAM64, CP-OFDM, DFT-s-OFDM, OTFS-like, AFDM-like and DL-NOMA-QPSK.• SNR range: −20 to +18 dB in 2 dB increments, with 1,000 observations per class/SNR combination.• Dataset size: 200,000 observations, each containing 256 complex samples represented as float32 I/Q with shape (2, 256).• Controlled simulation: shared settings for filtering, transmitter nonlinearity, time-varying multipath, carrier-frequency offset, phase noise, I/Q imbalance, amplitude variation, receive-window uncertainty and complex AWGN.• Fixed benchmark split: 160,000 training, 20,000 validation and 20,000 test observations, corresponding to 800/100/100 observations per class/SNR combination. Split seed: 2026. Data Format The dataset is supplied directly as a single HDF5 file, 6G-HW10.h5: X: I/Q observations, shape (200000, 2, 256), float32.Y: Integer class labels, shape (200000,), int16, values 0–9; these are not one-hot labels.Z: Nominal SNR in dB, shape (200000,), int16.class_names: The fixed class-label mapping.snr_values_db: The 20 nominal SNR levels.splits: Original zero-based training, validation and test indices.sample_metadata: 29 aligned generation-diagnostic arrays.metadata: Generation settings, field descriptions and source checksums. All signal values, labels, fixed split indices and per-sample metadata are preserved through lossless conversion from the frozen source dataset. README.txt explains the data structure, generation settings, scope and Python loading procedure. No ZIP extraction is required. Design Goals and Applications The dataset supports comparisons of heterogeneous signal classifiers, studies of representations for short I/Q observations, and evaluation across controlled SNR conditions. The fixed samples and split allow comparisons under the same benchmark conditions. Diagnostic metadata are not default inputs to the I/Q-only classification task. Research Context “6G-oriented” identifies the research motivation and selected waveform families. OTFS and AFDM have been investigated as candidate waveforms for next-generation wireless systems [1,2]. Here, OTFS-like and AFDM-like denote the implemented research constructions. The data are controlled synthetic observations, not standardized 6G air-interface transmissions or over-the-air measurements. No particular physical sampling rate, carrier frequency or mobility scenario is established. The two-file edition provides data and the fixed split, without the original generator or model-training code. References [1] M. Nie et al., “Towards Standardizing OTFS: A Candidate Waveform for Next-Generation Wireless Networks,” arXiv:2601.15048, 2026 (preprint). https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15048 [2] H. S. Rou et al., “Affine Frequency Division Multiplexing (AFDM) for 6G: Properties, Features, and Challenges,” IEEE Communications Standards Magazine, DOI: 10.1109/MCOMSTD.2025.3643183. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21704 Licence The dataset and README are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0). Attribution is required, and commercial use is not permitted under this licence. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

title: AI MATHEMATICAL DISCOVERY & INTERGENERATIONAL KNOWLEDGE EVOLUTION AT THE LIMIT A High-Density Research-Design Monograph on AI Reasoning, Formal Verification, and Mathematical Knowledge Succession STARLI | White Rainbow Civilization Mathematical Frontier Trilogy — Volume III Research-design edition | 13 October 2026 DESCRIPTION How can mathematical research remain inspectable, reproducible, corrigible, and useful to future generations when artificial intelligence participates in conjecture formation and proof discovery? This independently authored research-design monograph investigates this question through a three-component framework: AI Mathematical Reasoning × Formal Verification × Intergenerational Knowledge Evolution. Volume III completes a planned trilogy by shifting the focus from mathematical proof structures (Volume I) and cross-domain structural synthesis (Volume II) toward the institutions, formal artifacts, epistemic boundaries, and preservation methods needed for responsible AI-assisted mathematics. It proposes research protocols rather than claiming to establish new mathematical theorems. The monograph comprises 82 thematic chapters, each with one chapter-opening research relation and 12 individually paginated research units. Its six parts address: (I) research-oriented AI mathematical reasoning; (II) Lean, proof objects, and formal verification; (III) mathematician–AI collaboration and independent review; (IV) conjecture generation and counterexample search; (V) mathematical knowledge graphs, provenance, and proof archaeology; and (VI) long-term mathematical succession, model retirement, and open research governance. The final sections present 200 numbered Research Gates (G401–G600 in the trilogy-wide sequence) and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Research Gates are designed as executable entrances into unresolved work: each specifies an open question, a proposed test, an adversarial or stopping condition, and the evidence required for independent reassessment. The Answer Embryos are provisional research instruments that can be falsified, repaired, branched, or retired. A separate workbook indexes the chapters, research units, gates, candidate answers, and equation cards. The opening scientific preface contains 30 high-level physics derivation-route cards accompanied by conceptual three-dimensional geometric studies. Each of the 200 Research Gates and 33 Answer Embryos includes one distinct physics equation card, for a total of 233 equations. These retain their meaning within their original physical regimes; they are not presented as proofs of the book's claims about AI systems or mathematics. PRIMARY-SOURCE CONTEXT AND SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARIES The publicly available OpenAI Mathematics repository lists 719 manuscripts grouped into 372 families as of the public README consulted on 13 October 2026. These figures describe the reference catalogue and do not imply that this monograph has read or independently validated all underlying proofs. Repository content has varied in public versions; manuscript-specific claims should always be checked against their primary texts, available formalizations, citations, and version histories. Formal verification of an encoded theorem is not equivalent to proving that the encoded statement perfectly captures the original informal claim. Likewise, mathematical plausibility, numerical experiments, AI consensus, and persuasive exposition are not substitutes for deductive proof. The work is independent of OpenAI. It does not assert ownership of the original repository manuscripts, certify their correctness, or claim empirical results for the proposed research protocols. Its central contribution is an explicit research architecture in which negative findings, source corrections, independent reproduction, rights boundaries, and the freedom of successor investigators to challenge or replace earlier conclusions are treated as first-class scholarly artifacts. A mathematical civilization is not sustained merely by saving documents. It is sustained when future researchers can reconstruct the precise statement, revisit the evidence, inspect the dependencies, reject an invalid inference, and open a better question. PRIMARY REFERENCE https://github.com/openai/math https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/CONTENTS.md Publication note: This research monograph is a speculative methodological and interpretive research compendium, not a peer-reviewed certification of 719 mathematical manuscripts and not an official OpenAI release.

title: Calibration, Conformal Uncertainty, and Fairness of Large Language Models for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction after ICU Admission: Evaluation on MIMIC-IV with External Validation on MIMIC-III
abstract: This is a preregistered retrospective, non-interventional prediction-model evaluation using publicly available de-identified ICU data (MIMIC-IV v3.1 and MIMIC-III v1.4). We do not train or fine-tune large language models (LLMs). The study evaluates three axes of LLM-based in-hospital mortality prediction: calibration, conformal uncertainty, and subgroup fairness, with external validation. Structured first-day (0–24 h) ICU features are converted into fixed clinical vignettes. A primary LLM (deepseek-v4.1-flash) outputs an integer probability (0–100) of in-hospital death. Baselines include XGBoost, logistic regression, and SOFA. The confirmatory analysis uses a pilot-excluded cohort (n≈55,223) to avoid bias from previously observed pilot samples (12,000 stratified batch + 200 probe). The full cohort (n≈67,423) is reported as a sensitivity analysis. Primary estimands: (1) calibration via ECE (equal-frequency 10 bins) and calibration slope before/after Platt scaling; (2) conformal prediction using LAC (Least Ambiguous Set-Valued Classifier, Sadinle et al.) with target coverage 90%/95%, reporting empirical coverage and prediction set sizes; (3) subgroup fairness (sex, age, race_group including UNKNOWN_LIKE) via ΔECE and equalized odds gap. External validation applies locked calibration and conformal thresholds from MIMIC-IV directly to mapped MIMIC-III without retraining. Reporting follows TRIPOD+AI. Expected outcomes: a methodological assessment of whether LLM mortality probabilities are well-calibrated, whether LAC provides clinically interpretable uncertainty sets, and whether subgroup disparities exist. Exploratory pilot results (DeepSeek n=12,000; MiMo n=4,000) are disclosed as non-confirmatory and are excluded from the primary analysis. Preregistration lock date: 2026-10-13 (Asia/Shanghai). No institutional PHI; CITI/PhysioNet training completed.

title: Nonlocal effects via local quantum Fisher information: characterizations and interpretations
abstract: Abstract We introduce a quantum Fisher information based measurement-induced nonlocality (QFI-MIN), which quantifies the maximal statistical distinguishability induced by locally invariant unitary dynamics. The proposed measure inherits desirable properties including positivity, local unitary invariance, monotonicity under local operations, and immunity to the local ancilla problem. Analytical expressions are obtained for pure states, arbitrary two-qubit states, and two-qubit X states, revealing a direct connection with entanglement for pure systems. The proposed measure admits direct operational interpretations in local channel discrimination and quantum parameter estimation. Specifically, QFI-MIN quantifies the maximal infinitesimal distinguishability and parameter-estimation sensitivity achievable through locally invariant unitary encodings. Its behavior under amplitude damping, depolarizing, and generalized amplitude damping channels demonstrates robustness against environmental noise. The proposed framework provides an operationally meaningful quantifier of quantum correlations, establishing a direct connection between nonlocality, quantum metrology, and quantum information processing.

title: Federated learning with update level noise perturbation and blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving healthcare ECG classification
abstract: We propose FedChainDP, a federated learning framework that combines update-level noise perturbation with blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving collaborative ECG classification across multiple healthcare institutions. Healthcare institutions face a fundamental tension: deep learning models require large, diverse training datasets to achieve high diagnostic accuracy, yet strict privacy regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR restrict the sharing of raw patient data across organizational boundaries. FedChainDP resolves this tension by enabling hospitals to collaboratively train a shared CNN model without exchanging raw electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Each hospital trains locally on its private data and shares only noise-perturbed model updates, to which Gaussian noise is added once per federated round; these updates are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before transmission and logged on an immutable blockchain with Merkle-tree integrity protection and smart-contract policy checks on the reported noise parameters. Because this round-level noise schedule does not satisfy the assumptions of the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, the accountant output for the main configuration (ε_nom = 7.84 at δ = 10⁻⁵) is reported only as a nominal indicator, and no formal (ε, δ)-differential privacy guarantee is claimed. We evaluate FedChainDP on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia dataset partitioned across 5 hospitals using Dirichlet-based non-IID distributions. Our CNN model achieves 98.91% ± 0.14% accuracy under federated learning with update-level noise injection (σ_mult = 1.1), compared to 98.81% ± 0.31% for centralized training and 98.57% ± 0.17% for federated learning without noise-based privacy protection. These accuracies were obtained under a beat-level random split performed after duplication-based class balancing, so duplicated minority-class beats and beats from the same patients can occur in both training and test sets; they therefore reflect performance within this resampled benchmark and do not establish generalization to independent unseen beats or patients. A comprehensive privacy-utility analysis across noise multiplier settings (σ_multiplier ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 100}) demonstrates that classification accuracy remains above 98% across all evaluated noise levels. A black-box membership inference attack achieved 50.28% accuracy (near random guessing) against the noise-perturbed model; however, comparable near-chance accuracy was also obtained against the models trained without noise (49.16% centralized; 49.48% federated), so this result neither isolates a benefit of the noise mechanism nor substitutes for a formal privacy guarantee. A single-machine scalability simulation across 2 to 20 simulated hospitals produced accuracies of 98.90% (2 hospitals), 95.10% (5 hospitals), 93.80% (10 hospitals), and 97.20% (20 hospitals), respectively, while the simulated blockchain audit trail adds negligible overhead (0.059–0.091 s average mining time per block within the single-machine environment). FedChainDP incorporates technical safeguards relevant to healthcare privacy and accountability objectives across four dimensions: multi-technique privacy integration, blockchain-logged policy checks on reported noise parameters, smart contract access control, and empirical membership-inference evaluation.

title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.

title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning
abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.

title: Delegating Earth science model calibration to knowledge-guided LLM agents
abstract: Applying process-based Earth science models to new sites and questions often requires expert calibration decisions. Reliable delegation to language-model agents must preserve scientific competence and reproducibility. Here we develop a general calibration harness (GCH) for end-to-end delegation from a calibration request to assessed results. Constrained by a knowledge infrastructure (KI) and a validation convention, agents define parameter domains, observation mappings and objectives, and generate model-specific code. GCH checks the formulations against the same declarations and freezes them before numerical search and assessment, which require no further agent judgement. Agent-authored workflows executed across six model families, with assessment identifying unmet criteria. In snow-model tests, five of five knowledge-guided specifications executed on the first attempt, compared with none of five given only the model name, achieving validation Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.81-0.94 against 0.57 for defaults. Under a common objective, independent GR4J formulations yielded scores within 0.001 NSE; re-evaluating eleven saved parameter vectors reproduced their metrics. In ten paired VIC tests with matched budgets, fixed search was non-inferior to continuing agent proposals (margin, -0.02 NSE; median difference, -0.003). This separation enables end-to-end calibration delegation with inspectable scientific choices and reproducible numerical evaluation.

title: Collapse, Repair, and Drift: Dissecting Fine Tuning Dynamics in Speech Language Models
abstract: Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is commonly monitored through training and evaluation loss, but loss does not fully characterize how model functionality evolves along the same trajectory. We study this gap through dialect adaptation of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$. Character error rate (CER) reveals pronounced transient collapse and recovery whose severity and temporal structure are only weakly reflected by loss. Bidirectional layer patching reveals strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize during recovery. Pairwise gradient similarity alone does not reliably indicate optimization stability, whereas raw gradient spectral analysis provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization: successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, while failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent fluctuations. Finally, AdamW update transfer bypasses pronounced early collapse, yet substantial Mandarin degradation still emerges later in training. These results motivate three separable SFT dynamics: collapse, repair, and drift, and show that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation.

title: Frequency Routing and Identity Conditioning for Thermal-to-Visible Face Translation
abstract: Thermal-to-visible (T2V) face translation has important applications in nighttime biometric recognition, low-light surveillance, and human interpretation of thermal observations. The task remains challenging because thermal images do not directly record visible appearance, while the cross-spectral cues useful for reconstruction vary across frequency components and semantic roles. Existing spatially conditioned models tend to process these cues through a homogeneous adaptation path and do not explicitly separate local structure from global identity. We propose FreqID-Control, a parameter-efficient framework that organizes thermal guidance according to spectral reliability and semantic role while preserving the pretrained generative prior. It combines frequency-routed low-rank adaptation, which allocates separate transformation subspaces to low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail, with shared cross-spectral identity conditioning, which supplies compact global identity tokens independently of spatial thermal tokens. A controlled analysis on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces provides the empirical basis for this design, revealing stable low-frequency correspondence and edge-localized detail correspondence. Experiments on both datasets demonstrate strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation, while controlled ablations on MCXFace confirm the complementary contributions of frequency routing and shared identity conditioning.

title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

title: Delay Complexity Dimension: Learning with Delayed and Censored Labels
abstract: We study PAC learning of binary classifiers when labels arrive after random delays and are censored beyond an observation window $W$. How many samples does this observation model require? We propose a distribution-dependent answer, the Delay Complexity Dimension (DCD). The DCD combines the VC dimension with the exact label-information rate of the observation channel. Every learner needs $Ω(\mathrm{DCD}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. An oracle pseudo-label ERM matches this rate on the instance family of the lower bound, up to constants and logarithmic factors. On that family the DCD is within a constant factor of the classical censored-ERM complexity, and whether the DCD rate is achievable where the two separate remains open. The theory also yields a quantization scheme under which delay information lowers the residual label variance, an expedition policy with a $(1-1/e)$ guarantee for its version-space objective, and a phenomenon with no analogue in the no-delay setting. Under a fixed collection horizon, a moderate window can strictly beat immediate labels. Experiments on synthetic data and the Criteo conversion logs support these predictions. A budget-matched test of a companion labeler-diversity prediction is reported as a negative result.

title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.

title: Kolorektal Histopatolojide Tarayıcılar Arası Genellemede Frekans-Farkında Modüller ve Renk Normalizasyonu Stratejileri Gerçekten Katkı Sağlıyor mu? Çok-Tohumlu Bir Değerlendirme
abstract: Dijital patolojide farklı tarayıcıların yol açtığı alan kayması (domain shift), derin öğrenme modellerinin kurumlar arası kullanımını sınırlamaktadır. Bu soruna yönelik iki yaygın strateji — frekans-farkında mimari bileşenler ve normalize edilmemiş veriyle karışık eğitim — literatürde çoğunlukla tek koşumlu deneylerle olumlu sunulmaktadır. Bu çalışmada, kolorektal doku sınıflandırması bağlamında bu stratejilerin güçlü bir evrişimli sinir ağı (ConvNeXt-Small) taban modeline gerçek bir katkı sağlayıp sağlamadığı, üç tohumlu ve dış doğrulamalı kapsamlı bir protokolle sınanmıştır. Modeller NCT-CRC-HE-100K üzerinde eğitilip bağımsız CRC-VAL-HE-7K veri seti üzerinde test edilmiştir. Üç özgün bileşen — tarayıcılar-arası frekans normalizasyonu (CFN), doku-frekans ayrıştırma modülü (TFDM) ve uyarlanabilir füzyon (AFSM) — çıkarmalı (leave-one-out) ablasyonla; karışık ve normalize eğitim ise 2×2 tasarımıyla değerlendirilmiştir. Bulgular tutarlı biçimde olumsuzdur: taban modelin dış doğruluğu (%96.60±0.45), incelenen bileşenlerin hiçbiri eklendiğinde istatistiksel olarak anlamlı biçimde iyileşmemekte; CFN bileşeni dış doğruluğu sistematik olarak düşürmektedir (−0.70 yüzde puanı). Karışık eğitim, normalize eğitime kıyasla yalnızca +0.39 puan fark yaratmakta ve güven aralıkları tümüyle çakışmaktadır; hedeflenen zayıf sınıflarda (STR, MUS) dahi anlamlı iyileşme gözlenmemektedir. Sonuçları büyük ölçüde tohumlar arası varyans (±0.15–1.19 puan; tek-koşum yayılımı 2.2 puana ulaşmakta) belirlemektedir. Çalışma, bu kıyaslama kümesinde küçük mimari ve veri-stratejisi kazanç iddialarının önemli bölümünün tohum gürültüsüyle açıklanabileceğini göstermekte ve tek-koşumlu karşılaştırmalara karşı uyarmaktadır.

title: Weighted Proportional Conflict Redistribution for Heterogeneous LLM Ensembles
abstract: Smaller language models often exhibit high confidence in erroneous predictions, undermining traditional ensemble methods. In heterogeneous ensembles, simple averaging can grant disproportionate influence to overconfident but incorrect outputs. This paper introduces a reliability-weighted extension of the Proportional Conflict Redistribution rule (PCR6), where model-specific weights are derived from validation accuracy. We provide a formal treatment of the conflict measure, prove that the weighted rule avoids Zadeh's paradox in the high-conflict regime, and establish a quasi-associativity bound of order O(K_max²). We further justify linear weighting from both Bayesian (conjugate Dirichlet) and minimax perspectives, and compare the approach with logarithmic pooling and Dirichlet calibration. Empirical evaluation on a multi-model MMLU setting shows that the primary practical benefit of weighted PCR6 in our experiments lies in improved calibration (substantially lower Expected Calibration Error) rather than large accuracy gains over simple averaging. Accuracy improvements appear most plausible when ensemble members differ markedly in reliability; when models are comparably strong, the method remains competitive while producing better-calibrated probabilities. The fusion step itself is computationally lightweight (tens of microseconds per query for small ensembles).

title: dnf-composer: A C++ library and application for building and simulating Dynamic Neural Field architectures
abstract: Dynamic Neural Fields (DNFs) provide a mathematical framework for modeling continuous neural population dynamics that underlie perception, working memory, decision-making, and embodied cognition. **dynamic-neural-field-composer** (dnf-composer) is an open-source C++20 library and interactive application for composing, simulating, and visualizing one- and two-dimensional DNF architectures. ### What this capsule runs The Reproducible Run builds dnf-composer **v2.12.1** from source and runs three headless checks: 1. **Test suite** — the full GoogleTest suite → `results/test-report.xml`, `results/tests.log` 2. **Numerical validation** — 300 one-dimensional simulations (stimulus on for 500 steps, then off for 500 steps), saving activation profiles → `results/validation-1d/` 3. **Benchmark** — headless simulation throughput (steps/s) → `results/timings.csv` The interactive GUI needs a display, so it is not part of the Reproducible Run. Pre-built binaries and documentation: https://github.com/Jgocunha/dynamic-neural-field-composer

title: Posterior sampling of word embeddings
abstract: Abstract We study Bayesian inference for probabilistic word embedding models, including skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) and continuous bag-of-words (CBoW). These models are widely used for inference, but their posteriors are non-identifiable under general linear transformations, which prevents meaningful Bayesian uncertainty quantification. We provide a simple and principled identifiability constraint that yields a well-defined posterior without altering the data model. Building on this, we develop scalable, fully Bayesian posterior sampling algorithms for SGNS and CBoW using Pólya–Gamma augmentation. Our block Gibbs samplers yield exact samples from the posterior and scale well to large corpora due to their straightforward parallelisation. We discuss the efficient implementation of the Gibbs sampler, and provide a fast TensorFlow reference implementation. In a combination of simulations and empirical experiments, we demonstrate that the sampler is both accurate and computationally efficient. It matches the accuracy of NUTS-HMC at a fraction of the computational cost and avoids the variance underestimation of mean-field variational inference. On large real datasets, we show that posterior means yield improved predictive performance, while posterior credible intervals provide meaningful uncertainty quantification for semantic similarity.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Mineral Prospectivity Mapping with Positive-Unlabeled Learning and Conformal Calibration: Ni Mineralization in the Yilgarn Craton
abstract: Abstract Mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) supports exploration targeting, yet most machine learning approaches emphasize point probabilities with limited uncertainty quantification or coverage guarantees. Regional MPM faces incomplete deposit labels from biased exploration, spatial autocorrelation invalidating random cross-validation, and limited decision-relevant guidance linking probability surfaces to exploration priorities. This study develops a framework that combines positive-unlabeled learning, nested spatial block cross-validation, bootstrap ensemble uncertainty, and cross-conformal calibration, and converts the resulting signals into five priority zones defined by lift-based percentile thresholds and a 30% relative interquartile range ( $$\rho _{\text {IQR}}$$ ρ IQR ) cut-off. On the Yilgarn Craton, Western Australia (70,200 grid cells at 5 km resolution, 818 cells containing at least one known Ni deposit location, a 1.17% positive rate), the framework uses nested fivefold spatial block cross-validation with 50 km blocks informed by an empirical variogram. XGBoost and a BaggingPU-XGBoost variant achieve nearly identical outer test PR-AUC of 0.195 and 0.194 and ROC-AUC of 0.911, and the Excluded zone removes 9% of the positive cells at empirical coverage exceeding the 85% nominal target. BaggingPU-XGBoost produces more stable high-probability predictions, with median $$\rho _{\text {IQR}}$$ ρ IQR of 18% in the top 1% of bootstrap mean probabilities compared with 48% for XGBoost. This stability advantage shifts deposits into a more populated Immediate zone, so the combined Immediate and Priority zones of BaggingPU-XGBoost capture 33% of the positive cells compared with 23% for XGBoost. The framework provides an uncertainty-informed prioritization for MPM workflows in which discovery efficiency must be balanced against costs and investment risks.

title: Unmasking the Secret Code: Using Canaries to Show How Masked Context Controls Memorization in SFT
abstract: Canaries, or synthetic training records containing known secrets, are widely used to assess whether language models reveal information from their training data. But how much do these measurements depend on the canaries themselves? We study this question through controlled fine-tuning experiments with language and vision-language models, spanning synthetic tasks and tasks where training improves useful performance. Whether a secret is provided in the training input strongly changes what the model learns; for example, models can reproduce a secret in the input yet fail to recall it when it is removed, even after extensive repetition during training. When training instead requires predicting the secret from the surrounding context, later recall can become reliable. Repetition alone is therefore insufficient to characterize memorization. We also find that changing when a canary appears, or which other canaries accompany it, can substantially change measured memorization without increasing that canary's repetition count. These results show that canary measurements depend on how secrets are presented during training and tested afterward. Audits should test whether their conclusions hold across these choices before extending them to other training records.

title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.

title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

title: textGrain watermarking is harder to detect: can sum-tests still do it optimally?
abstract: Watermarking embeds an imperceptible signal in text from large language models that is statistically detectable with a secret key. The recent textGrain watermark (Li et. al. (2026b)) calibrates this signal against the model's sampling entropy through an explicit entropy budget, combining the stochasticity of Red-Green and the unbiasedness of Gumbel-max watermarks, and its accompanying report proposes a detector that sums pivotal statistics. We study when, and how efficiently, textGrain can be detected after human edits, modeled as a sparse mixture in which a fraction $\varepsilon_n\asymp n^{-p}$ of positions retain the watermark and token uncertainty decays as $n^{-q}$. First, entropy calibration comes at a cost: the minimax detection boundary of textGrain is $p+q=1/2$, so its detectable region is strictly smaller than that of Gumbel-max and maximal-coupling watermarks, whose boundary is $2p+q=1$. This cost stems from textGrain's construction rather than from entropy calibration itself: an unbiased scheme with the same entropy loss remains detectable where textGrain is not. Second, perhaps surprisingly, this loss makes the sum detector optimal at the boundary when the number of transport columns is fixed, unlike for Gumbel-max. When the number of columns grows and the entropy budget does not vanish, the detectable region expands while that of the sum detector does not. Third, for a fixed edit fraction, we characterize the optimal exponential rate of type II error decay and show that the sum detector falls strictly short of it at every fixed alternative. Finally, we propose a weighted multiscale binomial scan, valid in finite samples and needing no knowledge of the next-token distributions, entropy budget, or edit fraction; it attains every detection boundary above and the optimal exponent.

title: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models
abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.

title: Swiss4Arg: A Parallel Dataset for Multilingual Argument Mining across Swiss National Languages
abstract: We present Swiss4Arg, a multilingual dataset for argument mining based on official Swiss voting brochures, covering all four national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh (a Romance minority language exclusively spoken in Switzerland). The brochures contain explicitly formulated arguments systematically organized into pro and con sections, resulting in a cross-lingually aligned resource with balanced argumentative stance. We create a dataset that comprises 53 federal voting issues collected between 2019 and 2025, annotated for argument components (major claims, claims, premises, and non-argumentative units) and relations (support and attack) by three native speakers per language. Inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) reaches 0.548 for component classification and 0.623 for relation and target classification, computed jointly across all annotators on the parallel data. We release both adjudicated labels and individual annotator annotations, enabling analyses of disagreement and cross-linguistic variation, and provide baseline results using GPT-5.4 and SwissBERT. Swiss4Arg establishes a novel benchmark for multilingual argument mining, with a particular focus on cross-lingual comparability and low-resource settings such as Romansh. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://anonymous-hf.up.railway.app/a/gozw0nion72y/ (HuggingFace) and https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MultiVote-03BD/ (GitHub).

title: The Impact of AI-Enabled Customer Interaction on Consumer Buying Intention towards Housing Properties in Bangalore: Evidence from Adoption, Regression and Correlation Analysis
abstract: AI-enabled customer interaction, delivered through recommendation systems, chatbots and virtual assistants, is increasingly used by housing and real-estate platforms to engage prospective buyers. Housing is a high-value, high-involvement purchase in which trust and accurate information matter, yet evidence on how AI-enabled interaction relates to buying intention in an Indian metropolitan market such as Bangalore remains limited. This study examines the adoption and usage of AI-enabled customer interaction tools among prospective housing buyers, their impact on and relationship with buying intention, and the challenges buyers report. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted with a structured five-point Likert questionnaire, and 214 valid responses collected between 19 and 25 August 2026 were analysed with IBM SPSS Statistics and jamovi using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, one-sample t tests, multiple linear regression, and Pearson and Spearman correlation. Adoption was moderate-to-high (item means 3.26–3.48; composite = 3.373; α = .849). AI-enabled interaction was significantly and positively correlated with buying intention (Pearson r = .337; Spearman ρ = .349; p < .001). A regression of the five AI items on the outcome was significant but explained a modest share of variance (R² = .056; F(5, 208) = 2.490; p = .032), and no individual item was a significant unique predictor. The most prominent challenges were a preference for human interaction at final negotiation (M = 3.36) and technical issues (M = 3.27); the challenge scale was reliable (α = .792). Three of four hypotheses were supported and one was partly supported. The study extends AI-marketing research to the housing context and supports a hybrid AI-plus-human approach: AI for search and first enquiries, human contact for negotiation, and reliable technology throughout. Because the design is cross-sectional, the findings describe association rather than causation. KEYWORDS: AI-enabled customer interaction, Chatbots, Recommendation systems, Buying intention, Housing properties, Real estate, Bangalore.

title: Universal Fault-Tolerant Computation on Three-Dimensional Layer Codes at Optimal Distance
abstract: Three-dimensional layer codes combine local stabilizer checks with high storage density, butcomputation also requires local access to their logical operators. We give an explicit local realizationof the Williamson–Baspin layer code for any CSS input whose checks have weight at least two, withcomplete check matrices, and prove that it encodes exactly the input logical qubits, that everypure-X logical class has a representative supported on a single lattice layer, at every height ofthe block, and that every pure-Z class has one in a single transverse plane, at every position. Arunning (prefix) parity along each check sheet gives these representatives; a certificate on completecodes, with negative controls, checks every step. The slabs support logical Pauli measurementsby nearest-neighbor three-dimensional grid gauging. A constant number of ancillas per grid edgepreserves the full code distance, whereas a measurement layer of bounded thickness provably cannotpreserve it for the joint measurements that computation requires; complete circuit-level simulationsof a two-block measurement on explicit layer-code blocks of four sizes confirm both statements, withfailures through the thick grid falling and through a thin interface rising as the blocks grow. Withfully routed nearest-neighbor extraction, a one-row interface has fault distance one for three inputcodes, while on the smallest blocks the grid keeps the fault distance of idle memory. Lifting theinput distance through these slabs shows that the realization has the optimal distance Θ(N2) forgood inputs. Combining the measurements with encoded resource transfer, distillation, and a localdetector schedule gives a universal fault-tolerant architecture under local-stochastic Pauli noise. Atfixed noise below an existential threshold, a depth-T circuit on W logical sites in a bounded-aspectbox uses O(W f + f3/2) physical qubits and O(T f 3/2Ψ) ⊆ O(T f 5.41) depth in the minimal-spaceschedule, where f = Θ(log(W T /ε)) and Ψ = O(flog2 15) is the distillation depth factor; a concreteestimate with explicit allocations shows that the constants place the storage advantage at distancesof order a thousand. We also derive a fragmentation correction for general regions and port-packingbounds saturated by balanced layer codes.

title: Metrología y transferencia del campo confidence en modelos de decisión de pesos abiertos tipo Jev
abstract: Los modelos de decisión tipo Jev no generan texto:terminan la inferencia con un readout de logits y exponen uncampo confidence sobre el que el ecosistema fija umbralesde actuación. Sin embargo, el mismo nombre cubre definicionesmatemáticamente incompatibles. Este trabajo construye y publicaun instrumento para medirlo: la especificación formal de lasdefiniciones en uso, la librería jev-conf-metrics, un conjuntode 65185 decisiones medidas sobre pesos abiertos y una matriz detransferencia de umbrales que se regenera con un solo comando.Sobre 3564 celdas y 23 grupos (Laya en tres checkpoints, Kev0.8B y un control crudo), la diferencia entre la definición másalta y la más baja de la misma distribución tiene mediana 0.288;el porte directo de un umbral se equivoca del orden de cien vecesmás que el porte con el mapa cerrado cuando este existe; solodos pares de definiciones transfieren por identidad matemática;y la incompatibilidad es un fenómeno de n ≥ 3. El mismomodelo ofrece un ECE de 0.216 o de 0.577 según la definición.La contribución no es el hallazgo sino el instrumento: sobrevivea él y mide cualquier implementación futura.

title: ORAP-VIP: Reproducibility Package for Risk-Constrained Privacy Release Decisions in High-Value Customer Data
abstract: Overview This repository provides a reproducibility package supporting the research manuscript entitled “Risk-Constrained Privacy Release Decisions for High-Value Customer Data: A Synthetic Evaluation of Retention Constraints and Policy Agreement.” The study investigates privacy-aware data release decisions for high-value customer (VIP) subgroups in large-scale service environments. The experimental evaluation uses exclusively synthetic customer records and does not include real customer or expressway transaction data. Experimental Design Two risk-constrained privacy release policies are compared: B4: A baseline release-selection policy using calibrated disclosure-risk thresholds. SCRA-VIP: A retention-constrained policy using the same risk screening and utility ranking, with an additional minimum retention requirement of 20%. The confirmatory evaluation comprises 400 independently generated synthetic worlds across four scenarios (S0–S3), with 100 worlds per scenario and 30,000 synthetic customer records per world. Key Results All 400 synthetic worlds passed the recorded validation checks. No release-selection disagreements, false-safe selections, or abstentions were observed under the specified synthetic attacker model. The minimum observed retention among B4-selected releases was approximately 85.39%, exceeding the 20% retention requirement. Consequently, the additional SCRA-VIP retention constraint was non-binding in all evaluated worlds. These results characterize a policy-agreement regime under shared calibrated-risk screening. They do not establish superior privacy calibration, formal policy equivalence, or robustness against previously unseen attacker knowledge. Repository Contents The archive includes Python source code, experimental configurations, synthetic-world results, statistical analysis outputs, validation evidence, SHA256 manifests, and reproducibility documentation. Reproducibility and Limitations The released materials support verification of the reported synthetic experiments. Independent reproduction in a new computing environment has not yet been demonstrated. The VIP designation is a research-defined synthetic customer lifetime value (CLV) proxy rather than a verified business classification. title: FisherShield: Sequential D-Optimal Anti-Rewards for Deployment-Time Reward Privacy in Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning is increasingly deployed in autonomous systems whose reward functions encode operational priorities and decision-making objectives. However, observable behavior can enable external observers to infer sensitive reward parameters through inverse reinforcement learning. Existing deployment-time defenses mainly rely on action randomization or deception, without explicitly accounting for how previously released behavior affects the additional reward-sensitive information contributed by subsequent actions. To address this gap, we propose FisherShield, a deployment-time mechanism that balances task value against marginal reward-information exposure. Under a specified reference observer model, FisherShield computes the sensitivity of action log-likelihoods to the private reward and accumulates the sensitivity directions of released actions in an empirical information matrix. For each candidate action, the increase in the matrix’s log-determinant measures its marginal reference-score exposure and is converted into a weighted penalty subtracted from the task value. Updating the matrix after each release makes the penalty depend on the observation history, enabling sequential exposure control without retraining the task policy. Experiments show that FisherShield reduces cumulative reference-score log-det exposure by 26.4% in FourRooms and 34.3% in LavaGrid relative to Expert while preserving near-expert utility. The results are limited to the specified reference-model Bayesian observer and do not establish robustness to model misspecification or a defense-aware attacker.

title: SchemaPose: RGB-Based Category-Level Pose Estimation with Parametric Category Schema
abstract: RGB-based category-level 9D pose estimation remains highly challenging because a monocular system must generalize across unseen object instances while jointly inferring 3D translation, 3D rotation, and 3D size. Unlike instance-level pose estimation, the category-level setting requires the network to learn both what is shared across objects within a category and how individual instances vary in structure. This challenge is amplified in the RGB-only setting, where pose cues, category-level commonality, and instance-specific variation are entangled in appearance without direct geometric constraints, making it difficult for existing frameworks to learn a representation that is truly aligned with the category-level estimation objective. To address this problem, we propose SchemaPose, a schema-guided framework for RGB-based category-level pose estimation. SchemaPose equips the estimation pipeline with an explicit parametric schema for modeling category-level regularities together with structured instance variation, and uses the inferred schema variables to guide pose-related prediction in an end-to-end query-based framework. The same formulation also supports template instantiation, synthetic annotation, and pose learning within a unified framework. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that SchemaPose achieves state-of-the-art performance among RGB-based methods for category-level 9D pose estimation.

title: Shortcut in Generalization: Rethinking Evaluation Protocol for Encrypted Traffic Classification
abstract: Encrypted traffic classification is commonly evaluated under a range of experimental protocols, with classification performance reported as the primary measure. However, the reported performance may be influenced by shortcuts left uncontrolled in the evaluation protocol, such as shortcut features and cross-partition sharing, rather than reflect generalizable traffic patterns. And test-only feature transformations may further introduce train-test mismatch. In this paper, we study how current evaluation protocols are affected by shortcut-related factors, including field-level shortcuts, cross-partition sharing, and train-test processing. We compare feature importance, retrained feature removal, and field-only split sensitivity. We also vary Source-IP overlap and packets per flow, compare test-only IP transformations with matched train-test transformations. Experiments on three public datasets show that the performance of existing methods are affected by both cross-partition sharing and the consistency of train-test transformations. Specifically, increasing Source-IP overlap from 0% to 100% raises accuracy by about 32-33 points before identifier masking, compared with only about 8 points after masking. For two state-of-the-art pretrained models (i.e., YaTC and NetMamba), the 11-13 points loss caused by test-only IP zeroing is almost fully recovered when the same transformation is applied during both training and testing.

title: DVTR-KD: Distilling Vision-Language Models via Intermediate Visual Token Reconstruction
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.

title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
